meta.title: Who really said "What you do speaks so loudly that I cannot hear what you say"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Emerson wrote "What you ARE stands over you the while, and thunders..." in Social Aims (1875). The famous "what you do" version is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What you do speaks so loudly that I cannot hear what you say'?
meta.ogDescription: Emerson's real line says what you ARE, not what you DO. Quote Investigator traced the swap to a sermon published in 1900 — eighteen years after he died.

answer.label: Not Emerson’s words — a later paraphrase of Emerson
answer.authorDates: 1803–1882 · American essayist, lecturer & leader of Transcendentalism
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Emerson’s, but the wording is not. In “Social Aims” (Letters and Social Aims, 1875) he wrote: “Don’t say things. What you are stands over you the while, and thunders so that I cannot hear what you say to the contrary.” The popular one-liner is a streamlined 20th-century paraphrase — and it swaps the very word Emerson italicised, turning are into do.

source.heading: What Emerson actually published

docMeta.dd: Boston: James R. Osgood and Company, 1875

No known Emerson text carries this wording; earliest documented 1900

source.excerpt: When people come to see us, we foolishly prattle, lest we be inhospitable. But things said for conversation are chalk eggs. Don’t say things. What you are stands over you the while, and thunders so that I cannot hear what you say to the contrary. A lady of my acquaintance said, “I don’t care so much for what they say as I do for what makes them say it.”
trail: 1875 — the real sentence. Emerson publishes “Social Aims” in Letters and Social Aims (Boston: James R. Osgood and Company). The first-edition text ↗ reads: “Don’t say things. What you are stands over you the while, and thunders so that I cannot hear what you say to the contrary.”

1887–1896 — the compression begins. Quote Investigator ↗ documents a run of progressively shorter variants, all credited to Emerson — an 1887 newspaper report of his conversation, an 1890 sermon by Charles M. Southgate reading “What you are speaks so loud I can not hear what you say,” and others.

1900 — “are” becomes “do.” Per QI ↗, the earliest known “What you do” version appears in John Barnett Donaldson’s sermon “The Life That Lasts” (Minneapolis: North & West Publishing Co., p. 205): “‘What you do speaks so loud,’ said Emerson, ‘that I cannot hear what you say.’”

Today — the paraphrase wins. Wikiquote ↗ lists the genuine “Social Aims” sentence among Emerson’s sourced quotations and flags the condensed form as a variant — but it is the condensed form that circulates.
source.excerptNote: The italics on say and are are Emerson’s own, preserved in the 1875 first edition. They mark the contrast the famous paraphrase destroys: Emerson is opposing being to saying, not doing to saying.

author.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
author.heading: Emerson wrote the idea — someone else wrote the sentence
author.bio: Ralph Waldo Emerson was an American essayist, lecturer, philosopher, minister and abolitionist who led the Transcendentalist movement of the mid-19th century. A former Unitarian minister who left the pulpit for the lecture circuit, he built a body of aphoristic prose — Nature, Essays: First Series, The Conduct of Life — so quotable that it invited exactly the kind of compression on display here. Letters and Social Aims (1875) was his last major essay collection, assembled with help from his daughter Ellen and his literary executor James Elliot Cabot.

misattribution.heading: A real Emerson idea in someone else’s words
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication pinned on a famous name — the underlying thought is authentically Emerson’s, and he published it. What went wrong is the sentence itself, which was compressed and reworded by other people over roughly twenty-five years while keeping Emerson’s name attached at every step.

items.why: Emerson’s published sentence is “Don’t say things. What you are stands over you the while, and thunders so that I cannot hear what you say to the contrary” — verified in the first-edition text of Letters and Social Aims ↗. No known Emerson text carries the “What you do speaks so loudly” wording, and QI ↗ concludes the punchy short forms “probably do not represent the words that Emerson spoke or wrote directly.”

items.who: An anonymous chain of preachers and editors
items.why: Emerson italicised are to contrast being with saying. The popular version replaces it with do, which shifts the point from character to conduct. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the “What you do” form no earlier than a sermon published in 1900 — eighteen years after Emerson’s death.

items.scope: The intermediate “What you are speaks so loud” variant
items.why: This commonly-quoted middle form is closer to Emerson’s meaning but still not his wording. QI ↗ dates it to an 1890 sermon by Charles M. Southgate, “Ahab’s Covetousness,” which already credits it to Emerson.

items.scope: “What you are stands over you and thunders, and denies what you say”
items.why: An 1887 Michigan newspaper printed this as an unpublished saying taken from conversation between Emerson and C. J. Woodbury. QI ↗ allows that Emerson might have used this form in talk, but it is a second-hand report, not a text he wrote.

misattribution.truthLine: Emerson wrote the thought, in 1875, about what you are. He did not write the sentence the internet gives him — per Quote Investigator ↗, the punchy modern forms “probably do not represent the words that Emerson spoke or wrote directly.”

context.heading: Character, not conduct
lead: Emerson’s sentence sits in a passage about the emptiness of small talk. “When people come to see us, we foolishly prattle, lest we be inhospitable,” he writes. “But things said for conversation are chalk eggs.” Then the line: don’t say things — what you are is already thundering over the conversation, drowning out anything you might claim to the contrary.

The paraphrase quietly rewrites that. Emerson italicised the contrast between saying and being: his subject is character, the self that leaks out regardless of intent. The popular version substitutes doing, converting a Transcendentalist claim about the visibility of the soul into a brisk maxim about actions versus words. It is a serviceable proverb about hypocrisy. It is not what Emerson was arguing.
context.detailsSummary: How the sentence shrank, decade by decade
detailsBody: Quote Investigator lays out the compression as a sequence. Emerson’s 1875 original runs to two clauses and a qualifier. By 1887 a Michigan newspaper printing purported “unpublished sayings” from Emerson’s conversation had it as “What you are stands over you and thunders, and denies what you say.” An 1890 sermon tightened it to “What you are speaks so loud I can not hear what you say.” By 1900 another sermon had swapped in “do.”

Each step is a plausible act of quotation from memory, and each one is credited to Emerson. What survives into modern quote books is the end of that chain, not its beginning — which is why the version everyone knows is the one Emerson is least likely to have uttered.
context.pull: Emerson italicised are. The famous version replaces exactly that word.
